doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Learning to keep a gig and applying himself to different leaders
summary: Stewart explains playing what each leader needs, from Howard Johnson's gigs to Frank Foster and Globe Unity, and that Dixieland and free playing both require listening.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Well those jazz teachers/professors who haven’t done the gigs and all that, I think they don’t know how to teach a student how to play a gig. That’s part of it for me. That has to be — you can play all these things you’ve learned but how do you play a gig?
How to play a gig or how to keep a gig.

You know how to do I play to keep a gig? You know what I mean? Because you may play a gig and get fired right afterwards, but how do I play — I mean I had to learn that, there’s a bunch of work that I’ve done that — it was Howard Johnson’s gig before I played it. And I’m not saying, I don’t play — I don’t even begin to play what I think of as better than Howard Johnson by any stretch of anybody’s imagination because Howard Johnson is this genius musician. And I’m not just saying tuba player. He’s this genius musician that arranges, he plays anything he picks up, electric bass, tuba, baritone saxophone, pennywhistle, you know what I mean? But when I play for someone I play for them what they would ask me to play if they could think of it. So therefore everything I play — oh yeah, Bob, yeah that’s great, leave that in. So they trust me. And so I can apply myself to them, very personally think about what it is they want in this band and not just bring my politic to their band. And I definitely have a politic but I don’t — I bring it, but I temper it with what they need in their band. And quite often, more often than not, they never tell me not to play extra things I might put. Just like when I started playing with a bass player [scats] it grew from that. And so Carla Bley would hire me and Howard said, “Man I’m not sending you in to sub anymore, you keep taking my damn gigs man.” But that’s my, I kind of become these people. And that may have also to do with earlier we spoke about the hats you know, where I understand those different genres of music so I can apply myself to them in a certain way that they appreciate. Because Frank Foster didn’t have a really great appreciation for the free players particularly, but I could work with him and the free players. You know, I worked with Globe Unity which was a European free playing band and I understood how to do that. So I mean I don’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

really see a big difference between Dixieland and playing free improv. I really don’t. Because I do both and I know both require big ears. You have to listen. You have to listen. And what you then do is you’re either playing inside a tonality or you’re playing outside of any tonality. But what you play has to do with what’s going on. You see what I mean? And those rules apply to both of those musics. So it’s about listening.
